High time, high time. A high old time we had of it last summer? I overstate. But getting out the maps… Look! Up the valley of the Brenne, Louise de la Vallière… Syntax collapses. High time for that, high time. To Château-Renault, the tannery town whose marquis Rooke and James Butler whipped in Vigo Bay Or so the song says, an amoral song Like Ronsard’s where we go today Perhaps, perhaps tomorrow. Tomorrow and tomorrow and… Get well! Philip’s black-sailed familiar, avaunt Or some word as ridiculous, the whole Diction kit begins to fall apart. High time it did, high time. High time and a long time yet.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Spring, Time, Vernal

outputs.L1:
“Stooped to truth and moralized his song.”

Spring pricks a little. I get out the maps.  
Time to demoralize my song—high time.  
Vernal, a little. Primavera.  
First green, first truth, and last.  
High time, high time.

A high old time we had of it last summer?  
I overstate. But getting out the maps…  
Look! Up the valley of the Brenne,  
Louise de la Vallière…

Syntax collapses. High time for that—high time.  
To Château-Renault, the tannery town  
whose marquis Rooke and James Butler whipped  
in Vigo Bay—or so the song says:  
an amoral song, like Ronsard’s,  
where we go today.

Perhaps, perhaps tomorrow.  
Tomorrow and tomorrow and… Get well!  
Philip’s black-sailed familiar, avaunt—  
or some word as ridiculous. The whole  
diction kit begins to fall apart.  
High time it did, high time.

High time, and a long time yet, my love!  
Get out that blessed map.  
Ageing, you take your glasses off to read it.  
Stooping to truth, we potter to Montoire.

High time, my love.  
High time, and a long time yet.
outputs.L2:
“He lowered himself to truth and turned his verse into a lesson.” Spring has a faint sting, so I unfold the maps. It is time—well past time—to strip my song of its moral purpose. Slightly vernal. Primavera. The earliest green, the first truth, and the final one. Long overdue, long overdue. Did we have a grand old time last summer? That is an exaggeration. Still, as I open the maps—see! Along the Brenne valley: Louise de la Vallière. Sentence structure gives way. About time it did; more than time. Onward to Château-Renault, the town of tanneries, whose marquis was defeated by Rooke and James Butler in Vigo Bay—or so the song reports, a song without morals, like Ronsard’s, toward which we travel today. Maybe today; maybe tomorrow. Tomorrow, then tomorrow, then—

Recover! Be gone, black-sailed companion of Philip—or whatever equally absurd command applies. The entire apparatus of diction starts breaking into pieces. It was due to happen; long overdue. The moment has come, my love, though much time still remains. Bring out that blessed map. As age advances, you remove your spectacles to make out its details. Bending toward truth, we make our slow, fussy way to Montoire. It is time, my love—high time, with a long while still ahead.
outputs.L3:
The speaker welcomes the arrival of spring as a signal to unfold the maps and set out on a journey. The changing season brings not only renewal but also restlessness: it is an invitation to leave familiar surroundings, imagine possible routes, and turn geography into a field of poetic exploration.

Throughout the poem, the repeated call for a “demoralizing” song suggests a deliberate loosening of order. Syntax begins to fracture, diction becomes unstable, and conventional meanings give way to unexpected associations. Rather than offering a clear or uplifting message, the poem allows language itself to wander. This verbal disorientation mirrors the proposed journey, in which destinations matter less than movement, discovery, and the freedom to depart from established paths.

Literary and historical references mingle with specific place names, including the Brenne valley, Château-Renault, and Montoire. The result is a layered landscape in which cultural memory, personal experience, and physical geography overlap. These locations are not merely points on a map; they become part of a broader imaginative itinerary shaped by history and literature.

The recurring phrase “high time” gives the poem a strong sense of urgency. It implies that the journey should begin without delay, while also acknowledging the steady passage of time. The phrase therefore carries both excitement and unease: there is still time to travel, love, and explore, but that time cannot be taken for granted.

This tension culminates in the closing image of ageing lovers reading a map together. The scene is intimate and tender, yet it also faces the truth of mortality. Their shared attention to the map expresses companionship and a continuing desire for experience. Despite the awareness that they have grown older, the poem ends in hope—the hope that many routes remain open and that there is still “much time” left to share.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a spring journey through a landscape marked by French place names, but the movement is as much temporal and emotional as geographical. Each location becomes a point on a shifting map of memory, drawing the speaker back toward personal experience and outward toward the pressures of history. Spring conventionally promises renewal, yet here renewal is inseparable from aging and loss. The season’s freshness sharpens the speaker’s awareness that time is passing, that memories are unstable, and that any truth recovered from the past will remain partial.

Historical allusions deepen this tension. The places traversed are not neutral scenery: they carry traces of conflict, cultural inheritance, and earlier lives. Public history repeatedly intersects with private recollection, making it difficult to separate what belongs to the individual from what belongs to a broader collective memory. The poem therefore treats truth not as a fixed conclusion but as something encountered indirectly—in names, echoes, repetitions, and fragments of language. Memory preserves experience, but it also distorts, rearranges, and sometimes conceals it.

The form enacts this uncertainty. Repetition suggests both persistence and failure: words return because the speaker cannot leave them behind, but also because no single statement is sufficient. Wordplay produces multiple meanings at once, allowing sound and association to challenge straightforward explanation. At the same time, the syntax deliberately begins to collapse. Sentences break apart, connections become unstable, and diction seems to disintegrate under the weight of what the speaker is trying to express. This linguistic disorder is not merely decorative. It dramatizes aging, the erosion of certainty, and the difficulty of making experience cohere.

As the poem’s language loosens, its moral stance also changes. What initially resembles a moralized song—a poem seeking judgment, order, or a lesson—gradually becomes more intimate and less doctrinal. The speaker does not finally resolve the contradictions of truth and memory, nor does the poem offer a consoling philosophy of age. Instead, it arrives at an amoral acknowledgment of transience: time passes without regard for justice, intention, or human desire.

Yet this recognition is not wholly bleak. Love remains possible even when certainty fails, and discovery can continue despite age and loss. The journey’s value lies not in reaching a final answer but in continuing to attend to places, language, memory, and another person. Thus the closing sense that life and love may persist for “a long time yet” is both modest and hopeful. It does not deny mortality; it places against mortality the ongoing capacities to notice, remember, travel, and love.
outputs.L5: Spring arrives softly, turning the world green again. It is a time of renewal, when sunlight lingers, flowers unfold, and birds return with their bright morning songs. The vernal air carries the scent of rain and growing earth, inviting us to step outside and begin anew. In this hopeful season, time seems lighter—measured not by clocks, but by blossoms, warm breezes, and lengthening days.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, self-reflexive prose poem about aging lovers planning a spring journey through France with a map, using historical and literary allusions and the recurring phrase “high time.”
counterfactuals.output:
We spread France across the kitchen table, its blue rivers trembling beneath the salt cellar, its provinces folded into old wounds. Your finger follows the Loire; mine loses the road near Tours. Between us, the map opens like a second spring, green with promises the body has postponed.

High time, you say.

High time for Chartres, where the glass keeps its impossible blue and pilgrims once arrived with dust whitening their knees. High time for the gardens of Villandry, their hedges writing strict green sentences around the unruly verbs of roses. High time to stand beside the sea at Saint-Malo and let the Atlantic correct our breathing.

We are old enough now to mistrust itineraries. Caesar marched by one, Napoleon by another; both believed the road belonged to them. We will carry softer ambitions: two shirts, the good shoes, your pills in their small republic of compartments, my spectacles, this notebook that pretends it can preserve us. The map says distance in centimeters. The heart says otherwise.

Outside, February worries the bare branches. Soon Persephone will come back through customs, declaring nothing, though her luggage is full of narcissus and rain. Soon the cafés will set their chairs toward the sun as if attending a lecture on resurrection. We will take the train south, perhaps, through fields newly fluent in green.

High time.

You want Avignon, where the broken bridge still leans into its unfinished thought. I want Arles: the yellow rooms, the mistral, the Roman stones warmed by centuries of footsteps. We compromise on both, as lovers do after forty years—each surrender a minor victory, each victory sweetened by surrender. Somewhere near Les Baux we will misread a sign and quarrel. Somewhere under plane trees we will forgive the road for not being the road we meant.

I write “we will” and hear the grammar creak.

This poem knows what we know: the future tense is a courteous fiction. It lays out clean linen in a room no one has yet entered. Still, let it. Let language reserve us a table in Lyon, a narrow bed in Beaune, two cups in a station café. Let the sentence carry our bags upstairs.

High time to admit that we are not young travelers delayed, but old lovers departing.

At Vézelay, perhaps, we will climb slowly toward the basilica, pausing where younger selves would not have paused. Mary Magdalene will wait in stone, patient with our lungs. At Combray—or the village that lent itself to Combray—we may buy a madeleine and discover that memory is less obedient than Proust promised: no lost kingdom rising from the tea, only crumbs, butter, your hand brushing mine.

That will be enough.

We have had our wars, though no historian recorded them: the winter of your silence, the summer I packed a suitcase and did not leave, the long campaign against illness with its white corridors and barbarous fluorescent moons. We have signed treaties in bed. We have broken them before breakfast. We have watched our faces become the faces that once frightened us in family photographs.

High time to love those faces.

On the map, Paris is a starburst, all roads entering like questions. We will walk beside the Seine at dusk, if walking is what our walking has become. Notre-Dame, scorched and restored, will teach us the old lesson: ruin is not the opposite of continuance. The booksellers will close their green boxes. The bridges will hold their reflections loosely. Somewhere, Baudelaire’s swan will still be grieving a city that changes faster than the heart.

And we—what are we but a city rebuilt around damage?

I draw a circle around Paris, then another around you. The ink catches in the paper’s crease. No metaphor survives inspection, yet here I am making one: France as our remaining life, the roads as veins, the mountains as time’s stern weather, the Mediterranean as the blue margin where the poem must stop.

But not yet.

High time for lavender before it blooms, for vineyards before they leaf, for rain on the Dordogne, for cherries in a paper bag. High time to be lost without being abandoned. High time to sit on a bench in some unnamed square while spring rings every bell it has.

We fold the map badly. France disappears along its practiced lines.

Your hands, freckled and careful, rest over mine.

Tomorrow, we say.

High time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a modernist travel reverie set around the Brenne, Château-Renault, and Montoire. Include Louise de la Vallière, Ronsard, Vigo Bay, failing eyesight, and the refrain “High time, my love.”
counterfactuals.output:
The train entered the Brenne at evening, where the ponds lay among reeds like tarnished mirrors. Here and there, a heron lifted itself from the water with the grave reluctance of an old thought. The compartment glass gave back my face, superimposed upon poplars, telegraph wires, a white road dwindling toward some village whose name the guard had swallowed.

My eyesight was failing. Dusk began earlier for me than for others; signs blurred, stations arrived without consonants, and the world, once so sharply divided, flowed together—field into water, cloud into chalk, memory into desire.

“High time, my love,” you said.

Or perhaps the wheels said it: *high time, my love; high time, my love.*

At Château-Renault we descended beneath an iron roof. Rain polished the rails. The town climbed away in wet slate and pale walls, and I thought of Louise de la Vallière—not at court, not glittering beneath the king’s regard, but older, veiled, walking toward silence. What is a journey but the gradual exchange of one enclosure for another? Palace for convent, carriage for compartment, the bright tyranny of being seen for the dim mercy of vanishing.

You stood beside the luggage, though you had been dead five years.

“High time, my love.”

Beyond the station, the road bent through fields washed almost colorless. Somewhere Ronsard had praised a rose, a mouth, an hour that could not be detained. His syllables followed us southward, scattering petals over milestones. I tried to read them in the guidebook, but the print trembled and closed. I saw only the white margin, vast as winter.

At Montoire the Loir moved under the bridge with the composure of history. Houses leaned toward it, listening. There had been kings here, poets near here, treaties, betrayals, harvests, bells. Yet the river carried no explanations. It bore a leaf, then a splinter of sky.

In the hotel room a map was pinned above the washstand. I traced the roads westward with one finger until they reached the sea and Vigo Bay, blue in memory, though on the map it was merely a hook of coastline and a printed name. I remembered ships at anchor there, gulls turning in Atlantic light, your scarf snapping like a signal I had failed to understand.

Was that our beginning, or only the place where recollection now begins?

Night entered by degrees. The château vanished first, then the bridge, then my hands. Your face remained longest, because it had never depended upon sight.

“High time, my love,” I whispered.

The morning train would go on without us, past the Brenne’s dark waters, past Château-Renault and Montoire, past every station where the heart mistakes delay for permanence. Already, in the distance, a whistle opened the dawn.

“High time, my love.”

And we rose—or I rose alone—and went down toward it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, allusive prose-poem in the style of late twentieth-century British poetry, blending spring, old age, maps, French geography, naval history, Shakespearean echoes, and playful commentary on the poem’s own language.
counterfactuals.output: April, that unreliable cartographer, has coloured the hedges a provisional green and pencilled lambs in the margins, while I, old enough now to mistake weather for memory, unfold France across my knees: Brittany’s granite snout worrying the Atlantic, Normandy green with its long arithmetic of loss, the Loire loosening her silver hair through Touraine, and down below, beyond the blue-veined Massif, Provence rehearsing its loud vowels among olives. *Here be dragons*, naturally, though modern maps call them motorways. At Ushant the sea still keeps its black appointments. Howe’s ships shoulder through the fog of the Glorious First, every mast a stripped May-tree, every gun declaring—in the grammar peculiar to guns—that silence has been misunderstood. Nelson, not yet marble, closes one eye to improve the world; Villeneuve misreads the sentence; Trafalgar is punctuated in smoke. O, what a piece of work is man, to turn the horizon into a broadside, the broadside into history, history into a schoolboy’s ink-blot shaped like victory. Meanwhile the hawthorn foams beside the bypass, scandalously alive. I consult the legend—always a dangerous thing in poems—and discover that crossed swords mean battle, a dotted line uncertainty, a tiny blue anchor hope with two iron flukes. My hands, those estuaries, shake over Calais. Dover answers, chalk to chalk, like an old actor forgetting whether tonight he is Lear or the cliff. *Blow, winds*—but softly; the hearing aid complains. Somewhere in the Ardennes a cuckoo keeps bad time. Somewhere near Rouen, Joan’s ash enters the municipal flowerbeds and rises, greenly mistranslated. Paris is a black star with roads radiating like cracks in a mirror; Marseille opens its rough mouth to salt; the Rhône goes south as all good rivers and dynasties must. And spring? Spring is the poem’s most shameless word, already over-employed, turning up in primrose, bedspring, mainspring, spring tide—observe how language, given an inch of April, takes the whole blooming kilometre. I would revise it, but age has taught me revision is merely retreat with better maps. So let the daffodils signal from their little fleets; let each bee navigate by rumours of longitude; let the dead admirals pace their quarterdecks beneath the church floor, listening to rain tick its patient rigging. The year rounds Cape Winter under diminished sail. Ahead, perhaps, the orchards of Anjou are whitening; behind, the wake closes like a book. Yet one rook lifts from an English elm—there are still elms in poems—and crosses the Channel without passport, compass, or regard for metaphor, black as the word *black*, which is to say not black at all but feather, weather, distance, ink: a small republic of meanings, beating north by northwest into the extravagant light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine an elderly couple getting out their maps and considering a trip through the Loire Valley. Turn the scene into a fragmented monologue in which memory, history, and syntax unravel, ending with “High time and a long time yet.”
counterfactuals.output:
The maps came out after supper, though supper had been only soup, and the maps smelled of drawers, dust, the long blue sleep of folded rivers.

Here, she said.

Or here.

Her finger trembled between Tours and Amboise, not from indecision, he thought, but because all roads tremble when remembered.

We could take the old car.

The old car is gone.

Then the train.

Which train?

The one we took before.

Before what?

Before it was gone.

They bent closer. The Loire uncoiled beneath the lamp, pale as a vein under skin. Villandry, Chinon, Blois—names of kings, queens, staircases, murders behind tapestries, roses clipped into obedience. He remembered a courtyard full of rain. She remembered no rain. She remembered heat, white walls, his hand at her waist before his hand became this hand, knuckled, spotted, cautious among the glasses.

We stayed there, she said.

No, we meant to.

There was a room with shutters.

There are always shutters.

Green ones.

Blue.

And someone—who was it?—leaning over the well, calling down into the centuries. Anne, Catherine, Eleanor, the names fell in, struck no water.

He traced the road west. Saumur. Angers. The paper had split along a crease and the river vanished briefly into the wound.

We’ll need petrol.

We’ll need sleep.

We’ll need to find the suitcases.

The brown one has no clasp.

The blue one belongs to—

Silence belonged to them both.

Outside, a branch scraped the window, asking entrance, asking nothing. The clock went on assembling and disassembling the hour.

At Chambord, he said, there were more chimneys than days.

That isn’t true.

It ought to be.

Leonardo built the staircase.

Leonardo died elsewhere.

Everyone died elsewhere, except those who did not.

They laughed, then stopped, listening for the younger laughter that had once followed theirs, room to room, year to year. It did not come. Or came too softly.

Fold it this way, she said.

You’ll tear France.

France has been torn.

Not here.

Here especially.

The map resisted. North pressed into south, Orléans upon Nantes, battle upon vineyard, saint upon butcher, summer upon that winter when the pipes froze and they slept in coats and promised, promised—what?

To go.

To return.

To begin before arriving.

Her finger found the river again, downstream now, or upstream, the distinction weakening. Water going where water had gone. Castles rising and falling without moving. Their two heads above the paper, already portraits, already strangers studying the route taken by two strangers.

Tomorrow, he said.

If it’s fine.

If we wake early.

If the car.

The train.

The shutters.

The room.

Here, she said, though her finger rested on blank paper beyond the border, beyond any road the cartographer had troubled to name.

Yes, he said. There.

They did not fold the map. They let it lie open under the failing lamp, all that distance waiting, all that past ahead.

High time and a long time yet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
